wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for strawberry preserves: strawberries cooked with sugar, without added pectin.

akapity: NCHFP describes preserves as small, whole fruit or uniform-size pieces in a clear, slightly gelled syrup.
NCHFP uses 6 cups of prepared strawberries (about 2 quart boxes) and 4.5 cups of sugar, which makes about 4 half-pint jars.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.
Sterilize the jars and prepare two-piece lids according to the manufacturer's directions.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Choose large, firm, tart strawberries.
Wash and drain the berries and remove the caps.
Layer the fruit and sugar alternately and let them stand for 8 to 10 hours or overnight in the refrigerator or another cool place.
Heat the fruit mixture to a boil, stirring gently.
Boil rapidly, stirring as needed so it does not stick.
Cook to 9 °F (5 °C) above the boiling point of water, or until the syrup is somewhat thick, about 15 to 20 minutes.
Remove from the heat and skim.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
Fill the hot preserves immediately into hot, sterile jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Wipe the jar rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on two-piece metal lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 10 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
NCHFP says opened home-canned jams and jellies should be kept in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower; JarAtlas applies this to preserves too.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
NCHFP says to discard jams and jellies with mold on them, and USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest; JarAtlas applies this to preserves too.

Check an opened jar regularly for signs of spoilage such as mold, yeast or an off odor, including a fermented, yeasty or alcohol smell; if you find any, throw out the whole jar; NCHFP gives this for jams and jellies, and JarAtlas applies it to preserves too.
